1213-the-man-that-corrupted-hadleyburg:
Mark Twain tells of Hadleyburg, a town proud of its honesty, which a stranger corrupts with a single trick. He leaves a sack of gold with a note, to be claimed by the man who once helped him. Nineteen leading citizens, each sure he is the one, lie and scheme for the prize, and the town's fame collapses in public shame.

Twain's satire is cold and funny, and the exposure scene, with its letters read aloud, is a masterclass in comic justice. The tale runs short but hits hard. It stands as Twain's most savage joke about human virtue, and it still stings.
15768-the-gist-of-swedenborg:
A short guide to Emanuel Swedenborg, compiled by Julian K. Smyth and William F. Wunsch and issued by the Swedenborg Foundation in New York in 1920. Swedenborg, born in Stockholm in 1688, began as a scientist and later wrote on spirit and scripture. The compilers boil his large works down to key passages and plain notes. Readers new to Swedenborg get a door into a hard author.

A brief life opens the book, tracing Swedenborg from Upsala study and travel in Europe to meetings with Flamsteed and Halley. Extracts then set out his views on God, the soul, heaven and hell, and the inner sense of the Bible. The editors keep comment short and let Swedenborg speak. The result suits a reader who wants the core of his thought without tackling his many volumes.
17485-history-and-comprehensive-descript:
James W. Head published this history and full description of Loudoun County, Virginia, in 1908, dedicating it to his mother, whose love for Loudoun he calls no less ardent than his own. Head calls the book the single ambition and fondest achievement of his life. He opens by praising the county as an example of country life in about its purest and pleasantest American form, while denying that it is any sort of rural utopia.

The volume sets out the county's past, places, people, and ways of life in comprehensive detail. Readers get a local history written by a devoted native, useful for genealogy, for Virginia history, and for the look of a farming county at the start of the twentieth century. Its affection for its subject is plain on every page.
22990-historical-sketch-of-the-cathedral:
Strasburg Cathedral displays every epoch of Christian architecture in one building, says this Historical Sketch of the Cathedral of Strasburg. For the artist, the cathedral is a subject of serious study. For the inhabitant of Strasburg, it is a venerable monument recalling the principal events of the city's ancient history.

The sketch walks readers through the great church, its famous spire, rose window, and astronomical clock among the wonders. French and German hands both shaped the building, as they fought over the city itself. Guidebooks like this one served the nineteenth century's new tourists, hungry for Gothic facts. Its Strasburg keeps the older spelling and the older pride, stone by stone.
25603-detailed-minuti-of-soldier-life-in:
Carlton McCarthy writes this detailed account of soldier life in the Army of Northern Virginia from 1861 to 1865. He served as a private in the Second Company, Richmond Howitzers. W. L. Sheppard supplied pictures, and the book appeared in Richmond in 1882. McCarthy dedicates it to his brother Edward, a captain killed at Cold Harbor in June 1864.

Chapters open with a voice from the ranks, the outfit modified, and romantic ideas dissipated. Marching, cooking and eating, and comforts of camp follow, in a private's plain view of war. McCarthy writes from the ranks, not from headquarters, and small daily details carry the history.
25825-at-plattsburg:
Allen French writes At Plattsburg, published by Scribner's Sons in April 1917 and dedicated to Squad Eight. French warns the squad is not as it really was, with some members absent and the rest altered, since story needs and facts to display forbade true portraits.

Richard Godwin writes to his mother from a train nearing Plattsburg on Friday morning, 8 September 1916, noting her amused smile at parting. French hopes to show the thing in Plattsburg that meant most to him personally, the spirit of the squad, as young officers train for war in a citizen camp.
33121-the-battle-of-gettysburg:
Frank Aretas Haskell's Battle of Gettysburg is a first-hand account by an aide-de-camp to General John Gibbon and colonel of the Thirty-sixth Wisconsin Infantry. It was reprinted by the Wisconsin History Commission in November 1908 in twenty-five hundred copies. Maps of the battle on July 2 and July 3 accompany the text, with a portrait of Haskell as colonel. The commission, organized under Wisconsin law and including Governor James O. Davidson and historian Frederick J. Turner, issued it as reprint number one.

Haskell writes from the center of the Union line, describing the fighting he saw and the men beside him with the immediacy of a staff officer's letter. His account became one of the most quoted Union narratives of Gettysburg, valued for detail and for feeling. For students of the Civil War, it remains an essential primary source, vivid, direct, and grounded in a soldier's own ground.
4711-tom-swift-in-the-city-of-gold-or-ma:
Victor Appleton sends Tom Swift to the city of gold in this boys' adventure, subtitled marvellous adventures underground. It opens with wonderful news and a letter for Tom, the first mail he has had that week. Chapters follow an unsuspected listener, Andy whitewashed, a perilous flight, news from Africa, and a warning to beware the head-hunters. Tom makes a promise, Eradicate will go, and a face that looked like Andy appears.

Mysterious passengers, a midnight alarm, and a journey into the unknown lead to a weary search, a golden image, and a map on gold. A ruined temple, a tunnel, and an underground river bring Tom to the city of gold itself, with a big image, a trap, a fight, and an escape. Readers get a fast inventors' tale of lost cities, treasure, and danger underground, with Tom's machines and friends carrying the day.
bely-petersburg:
Andrei Bely set his great novel in the capital of Russia on the edge of revolt, and German readers receive it here in translation. A senator's son, drawn to nihilist ideas, is handed a bomb and a deadly task. The city itself feels alive, damp, and hostile.

Bely tells the tale in rhythmic, feverish prose full of sudden images. Father and son circle each other while plots thicken and time runs short. Critics often call the novel Russia's answer to Ulysses. It proved that Russian fiction could be bold, strange, and fully modern in form as well as theme.
britannica-1911-aalborg:
Aalborg receives a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The city and seaport sits on the south bank of the Limfjord in Denmark, seat of a bishop and chief town of its amt. Marshy lake shores and the Store Vildmose swamp frame the north Jutland scene.

Rails run north to Skagen and south toward Germany, and the harbour, hard to enter, is good and safe. Grain and fish go out; works and trade grow year by year. Old houses, a castle, and the Budolphi and Frue churches mark the past. Nörre Sundby faces it across an iron bridge. Town rights date to 1342 and the see to 1554, the entry notes, with 31,457 souls in 1901.
britannica-1911-abensberg: Abensberg is the subject of a short town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry sets the Bavarian town on the Abens, a Danube feeder, south-west of Regensburg, joined by rail. Its people numbered 2,202. A small spa draws visitors, its sulphur baths used against rheumatism and gout. The town stands as the Romans' Castra Abusina, and Roman remains lie near by. On the twentieth of April 1809, the entry closes, Napoleon won a signal victory there over the Austrians under Archduke Louis and General Hiller.
britannica-1911-agricola-georg:
Georg Agricola (1490-1555) was a German scholar and man of science. Bauer was his family name, Agricola its Latin form. Posterity calls him the father of mineralogy. He was born at Glauchau in Saxony in 1490. At twenty he taught Greek at Zwickau. Leipzig studies added medicine, physics, and chemistry. Italy gave him his doctor's degree. He settled as physician at Joachimstal, a mining town. Testing written mineralogy against ores was his aim.

System grew from that testing. His Bermannus of 1528 ordered practical mining knowledge scientifically. Chemnitz made him town physician and burgomaster. Protestant Chemnitz forced the Catholic Agricola out, though. His De re metallica appeared in 1556, after his death. Twelve books treat mining and metallurgy completely.
britannica-1911-albert-i-brandenburg:
Albert I, margrave of Brandenburg, surnamed the Bear, who lived from about 1100 to 1170, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Only son of Otto the Rich, count of Ballenstedt, he inherited his father's Saxon estates in 1123. Through his mother Eilika he later gained half the lands of the Billungs, an old Saxon house. Lothair of Saxony gave him the margraviate of Lusatia about 1123.

Disappointment over the Saxon north mark led Albert to attack its new margrave, and Lothair stripped him of Lusatia. Service in Italy restored his fortunes, and in 1134 he received the north mark itself. Three years of campaigns against the Wends followed, and an arrangement with Pribislaus of Brandenburg made him founder of the margraviate of Brandenburg. Given Saxony in 1137, he was driven out by Henry the Proud and gave the duchy up at the peace of 1142.
britannica-1911-albert-iii-brandenburg:
Albert III, elector of Brandenburg, surnamed Achilles, who lived from 1414 to 1486, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Third son of Frederick I of Hohenzollern, he was born at Tangermunde in November 1414. Time at the emperor Sigismund's court and war against the Hussites seasoned him young. He later helped the German king Albert II against the Poles.

When his father's lands were divided in 1440, Albert received Ansbach, and from meagre resources he rose to lead among German princes. He resisted towns seeking self-government and fought Nuremberg from 1448 to 1453, losing that contest. Succeeding his brother as elector, he brought Pomerania under his supremacy by the treaty of Prenzlau in 1472. His dispositio Achillea of 1473 decreed that Brandenburg should pass whole to the eldest son, with younger sons taking the Franconian lands.
britannica-1911-albrechtsberger-johann-g:
Johann Georg Albrechtsberger (1736–1809) taught some of the best-known names in music, Beethoven among them. Hummel, Moscheles, and Josef Weigl also learned from the Austrian master. His pull as a teacher of theory drew crowds of pupils to Vienna. Born at Kloster-Neuburg near the capital, he had studied how to compose with Mann, the court organist.

Counterpoint, the craft of weaving tunes together, was his strength, and few of his day knew more of it. Organ posts at Raab and Maria-Taferl came first; then, in 1772, he played for the Vienna court, and in 1792 he took charge of music at St Stephen's Cathedral. Most of his own pieces, preludes, fugues, sonatas, and quartets among them, rest in manuscript at Vienna. His deepest gift to music was his writing on theory: a 1790 book on composition ran to a third edition, and his works on harmony filled three volumes.
britannica-1911-annaberg:
Annaberg is a town in Saxony, Germany. It stands in the Erzgebirge mountains. Its altitude is 1,894 feet. The Bohemian frontier lies six miles away. Chemnitz is eighteen and a half miles north. Population reached 16,811 in 1905. Three Evangelical churches serve the town. St Anne's church, built 1499 to 1525, is chief. A Roman Catholic church also stands there.

Monuments honour Luther and Adam Riese. Riese was a famous arithmetician. Barbara Uttmann also has a monument. She introduced braid and lace-making in 1561. Belgian refugees developed that industry after 1590. Annaberg remains Germany's chief seat of lace-making. Technical schools teach the trade locally. Mining once made the town famous too. Tin, silver, and cobalt were its products. That mining industry has now ceased.
britannica-1911-baiter-johann-georg:
Baiter, Johann Georg (1801-1877), was a Swiss scholar of old texts. He was born at Zürich in 1801. Zürich gave him his early schooling. He studied at Tübingen from 1818. Lack of money drove him home again. He tutored privately for several years.

From 1824 Baiter studied at Munich, Göttingen, and Königsberg. Great teachers trained him at each place. From 1833 he taught at the Zürich gymnasium. He stayed there until 1876. Textual criticism was his great strength. He applied it chiefly to Cicero. The Attic orators shared his care. He hunted the best manuscripts eagerly. His collations were made with great accuracy. Most works came out with partners. Orelli called him his right-hand man. Their Plato and Cicero editions marked real advances.
britannica-1911-bamberg:
Bamberg is a town and archiepiscopal see in Bavaria, Germany, on the river Regnitz near its junction with the Main, 39 miles north of Nuremberg by rail. Its people grew from 31,521 in 1885 to 45,308 in 1905. The upper town crowns seven hills, each topped by a church, while the lower town keeps parts of its old walls.

The cathedral leads the 1911 Britannica entry: a late Romanesque building with four towers, founded by the emperor Henry II in 1004 and rebuilt after fire in the 13th century. Inside stands Riemenschneider's marble tomb of Henry and the empress Cunigunde, carved between 1499 and 1513. Other churches named include the Jakobskirche and the Michaelskirche on its hill.
britannica-1911-battenberg:
Battenberg is the name of a German family traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Counts of that name, seated at Kellerburg near Battenberg in Hesse, died out about 1314. The title slept for five centuries. It was revived in 1851. Alexander, a younger son of Louis II of Hesse, made a morganatic marriage, a match with a wife of lower rank, with the Polish countess Julia von Haucke. She was then made countess of Battenberg.

Royal links fill the next age of the name. In 1858 the countess rose to princess, and her children took the style of princes of Battenberg. The eldest son, Louis Alexander, wed Victoria, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria, and became an admiral in the British navy. One son ruled Bulgaria from 1879 to 1886. A third, Henry Maurice, wed Princess Beatrice, Queen Victoria's youngest daughter, and died on active service in the Ashanti War in 1896.
britannica-1911-berg:
Berg, in Latin Ducatus Montensis, was a former duchy of Germany on the right bank of the Rhine. Cleves bounded it north, La Marck and Westphalia east, and the bishopric of Cologne south and west. Its area ran to about 1,120 square miles.

The district became a countship in 1108 and a duchy in 1380 under the Jülich family, joining Jülich in 1423 and Ravensberg in 1437. When the male line died out in 1609, the fight over who should inherit helped feed the Thirty Years’ War. A partition of 1614 gave Berg to the Neuburg line; Napoleon later made it a grand duchy, and the congress of Vienna handed it to Prussia in 1815.
britannica-1911-bernburg:
Bernburg is a town in the duchy of Anhalt, Germany, on the river Saale, 29 miles north by west of Halle, and formerly capital of Anhalt-Bernburg. The 1911 Britannica entry gives 34,929 people in 1905 and describes four quarters: the old town, the hill town with its moated ducal castle, the new town, and the suburb of Waldau.

Its industries include machinery and boilers, sugar, pottery, chemicals, and lead and zinc smelting, with market gardening and a large river trade in grain. The hill town was fortified by Otto III in the 10th century, and the separate quarters were united only in 1824.
britannica-1911-bertold-von-regensburg:
Bertold von Regensburg (about 1220–1272) was a Franciscan preacher, a native of Regensburg in Germany. He entered the Franciscan house in his home town. From about 1250 his fame spread across German-speaking Europe. He wandered from village to town preaching in the open air. Enormous crowds heard him. He taught that true repentance comes from the heart. Pilgrimages and absolution, he said, were mere outward signs.

Seventy-one of his German sermons survive today. The 1911 Britannica entry ranks them among the strongest in the language. They are chief monuments of Middle High German prose. His style is clear and direct, free of heavy Latin turns. He used peasant sayings and rough humour to drive a moral home. He died at Regensburg in December 1272.
britannica-1911-boksburg: Boksburg is a mining town in the Transvaal, 14 miles east of Johannesburg by rail. Its municipality held 14,757 people in 1904, of whom 4175 were whites. The entry is short and is given over wholly to coal. Boksburg was the headquarters of the Witwatersrand coal trade. Its collieries ran eastward from the town to Springs, 11 miles away. Brakpan, the largest colliery in South Africa, lay midway between the two places.
britannica-1911-bromberg:
Bromberg is a German town in the Prussian province of Posen, 32 miles by rail west-north-west of the fortress of Thorn and 7 miles west of the Vistula's bank. It sits at the centre of a railway network of weight, tying it to strategic points on the Prusso-Russian frontier. Its people rose from 52,082 in 1900 to 54,229 in 1905, and a large garrison matches its border place.

Two Roman Catholic and three Protestant churches serve the town, with a synagogue, a seminary, high schools and a theatre. Statues honour the emperor William I and Benkenhoff, builder of the Bromberg Canal. That canal, dug in 1773-1774 by Frederick II's order, joins the Brahe to the Netze and so links Vistula, Oder and Elbe. Iron foundries, machine shops, paper factories and flour mills lead its works. Bromberg is mentioned as early as 1252 and was taken by the Teutonic Order in 1327.
britannica-1911-bronn-heinrich-georg:
Heinrich Georg Bronn (1800–1862) was a German geologist born on 3 March 1800 at Ziegelhausen near Heidelberg. He took his doctor's degree in medicine at Heidelberg in 1821 and the next year became professor of natural history there. From then he gave himself to palaeontology, the study of fossils, with fieldwork across Germany, Italy and France. He helped edit the Jahrbuch fuer Mineralogie from its start in 1830 until 1862.

His principal work, Lethaea Geognostica, two volumes issued at Stuttgart from 1834 to 1838, with a third edition alongside F. Romer, has been counted one of the foundations of German stratigraphical geology. His Handbook of a History of Nature from 1841 gave the earth's physical history, then its life history, with species treated as direct acts of creation. Its third part held his famed Index Palaeontologicus of 1848-1849, a fossil record of inestimable value to all later workers in the field.
britannica-1911-calenberg:
Calenberg is a district of north Germany, around Hanover. It was once part of the duchy of Brunswick. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives its outline. The district took its name from a castle. That castle stands near Schulenburg. The rivers Weser and Leine cross the district. Its area is about 1050 square miles. The town of Hanover lies within it.

The district passed to younger sons of the Brunswick house. One such cadet was Ernest Augustus. He later became elector of Hanover. From him descend the Hanoverian kings of Britain and Ireland. The entry is only a few lines long. It gives the district's name, rivers and size. It adds the line of princes who held it. That dynastic link is the point of the notice. Nothing further is claimed for the place.
britannica-1911-cherbourg:
Cherbourg is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a naval station and seaport of north western France, in the department of Manche. It stands on the English Channel, 232 miles west north west of Paris by rail. The town counted 35,710 people in 1906. It sits at the mouth of the Divette, at the head of the Cotentin peninsula. Apart from a fine hospital and the fifteenth century church of La Trinité, it has no buildings of special interest.

Cherbourg's weight lies in its harbours. The naval harbour has three main basins cut out of the rock, covering 55 acres, with at least 30 feet of water. Dry docks and building yards for the largest ships of the French navy stand with it. The town is a fortress of the first class. Its own industries include fishing, ship building, tanning, and rope making. Statues honour the painter Millet and Napoleon I.
britannica-1911-cobourg:
Cobourg is the capital of Northumberland county, Ontario, Canada, on Lake Ontario and the Grand Trunk railway, 70 miles east-north-east of Toronto. Its people numbered 4,239 in 1901, and it has a large, safe harbour for lake traffic. Steamboat communication links it with St Lawrence and Lake Ontario ports. Car works, foundries and carpet and woollen factories give the town its industry beyond the harbour trade.

Cobourg is also a summer resort, especially for Americans, the entry adds to its working account. That resort role sits beside foundries and factories in the short portrait given here. Victoria University was formerly situated at Cobourg in its earlier years. In 1890 that university was removed to Toronto, leaving the town without its college, a closing fact that marks the notice's date and the town's change.
britannica-1911-coburg:
Coburg is a town of Germany, twin capital with Gotha of the duchy of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha, on the left bank of the Itz, 40 miles south-south-east of Gotha. Its people numbered 22,489 in 1905, and the town is for the most part old, with many interesting buildings. The ducal palace, the Ehrenburg, was originally erected by Duke John Ernest in 1549 on a convent site. Renovations in 1698 and restoration in 1816 gave it its present form, with a vast decorated hall and picture gallery.

In the market square stand the medieval Rathaus, government buildings and a statue of Prince Albert, consort of Queen Victoria, by William Theed the younger. The Moritzkirche, with a lofty tower, is the most remarkable church in the town. A gymnasium founded in 1604 by Duke John Casimir, the Casimirianum, heads its schools. The armoury, or Zeughaus, contains the ducal library of 100,000 volumes.
britannica-1911-coorg:
Coorg is a small province of India on the plateau of the Western Ghats, sloping inland toward Mysore. Its name is an English corruption of Kodagu. That word is said to come from a Kanarese term for steep or hilly land. A commissioner runs the province under the resident of Mysore. Mercara, with 6,732 people, is its headquarters town.

Coorg is the smallest province in India, at 1,582 square miles. About 1,000 of those miles are ghat, reserved or other forest. It counts as a province for its isolation, not its size. The ghats cut it off from the British districts to west and south. Coffee grows well on its heights and draws planters. That trade has lost ground since 1891, the entry notes. Forest still covers the greater part of the land. More than 3,000 native Christians live there, and traders form a marked class.
britannica-1911-emmitsburg:
Emmitsburg is a town in Frederick county, Maryland, 61 miles by rail west by north of Baltimore and near the northern boundary of the state. Its population was 849 in 1900 and 1054 in 1910. The town stands in a pretty region on the eastern slope of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

Two miles south-west stands Mount St Mary's College, a Roman Catholic college founded in 1808 and chartered in 1830, whose seminary is called the “Nursery of Bishops.” Half a mile south of the town is St Joseph's College and Academy for young women, run by the Sisters of Charity. That order was brought into the United States at Emmitsburg by Elizabeth Ann Seton in 1809. The first settlement was made about 1773 under the name “Silver Fancy,” then “Poplar Fields.” The present name, honouring settler William Emmitt, was adopted in 1786, and the town was incorporated in 1824.
britannica-1911-frederick-i-elector-of-b:
Frederick I (about 1371-1440), elector of Brandenburg, founded the greatness of the House of Hohenzollern. A son of Frederick V, burgrave of Nuremberg, he first won fame by saving the life of King Sigismund of Hungary at Nicopolis in 1396. He became burgrave in 1397 and sole ruler of the family lands after his brother John died in 1420.

In the double election of 1410 Frederick cast the Brandenburg vote for Sigismund and did much to seat him as German king. Sent to govern Brandenburg, he restored order, and at Constance on 18 April 1417 he was formally invested as elector and margrave. He later fought the Hussites, sold his burgrave rights to Nuremberg in 1427, and in 1440 declined the crown of Bohemia. He died that September at Radolzburg.
britannica-1911-fredericksburg:
Fredericksburg is a city of Spottsylvania county, Virginia, on the Rappahannock river at the head of tide-water, about 60 miles north of Richmond. Its population was 5874 in 1910. A dam 900 feet long feeds a canal giving water power for flour, leather, shoes, woollens, and other goods. Washington mother died here in 1789, and Kenmore, home of her brother-in-law Fielding Lewis, still stands.

The city is famed for the battle of 13 December 1862. Burnside crossed the river with 122,000 men against Lee entrenched 79,000. On the right, Jackson line was pierced but held. At Marye Heights, division after division charged the stone wall on a narrow front and none reached it. Federal losses were 12,650 against 4200 Confederate, and on the night of 15 December the Union army withdrew across the river.
britannica-1911-freyburg:
Freyburg, or Freyburg an der Unstrut, is a town of Germany in Prussian Saxony, set in rolling vine country on the Unstrut river, six miles north of Naumberg. Its 3200 people worship in a parish church mixing Gothic and Romanesque work under a handsome tower. The town makes sparkling wine of good quality and a few other small goods.

Freyburg is best known as a place of pilgrimage for German gymnastic societies. Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, the father of German gymnastics, lies buried here, with the Turnhalle built over his grave and holding his statue, and the Jahn Museum of 1903 beside it. On a hill above the town stands the castle of Neuenburg, first raised in 1062 by Louis the Leaper and in its present shape mostly the work of the dukes of Saxe-Weissenfels.
britannica-1911-friedberg:
Friedberg is the name of two German towns treated in one entry. The first is a small town in Upper Bavaria with an old castle, known chiefly as the scene of Moreau victory over the Austrians on 24 August 1796. The second and larger is Friedberg in der Wetterau, in Hesse-Darmstadt, set above the Usa river 14 miles north of Frankfort.

The Wetterau town held 7702 people in 1905 and keeps its old walls and towers, a fine Gothic town church, an old castle, and a grand-ducal palace with a noted garden. Sugar, gloves, and leather are made there, with breweries besides, and the schools include technical and farming academies. Of Roman origin, it is first named as a town in the 11th century, became a free imperial city in 1211, changed hands often, and passed to Hesse-Darmstadt in 1802.
britannica-1911-galesburg:
Galesburg is a city of Illinois and the county-seat of Knox county, 163 miles south-west of Chicago, with 22,089 people in 1910. It is served by the Santa Fé and the Burlington railways. Knox College, chartered in 1837 and opened in 1841, and the Universalist Lombard College are its chief institutions, and a public library dates from 1874. Its industries centre on the Burlington railway car shops and on foundry products, vitrified brick and farm machinery, the factory output of 1905 reaching $2,217,772.

The city honours the Rev. George Washington Gale, who led the first settlers there in 1836 to plant a college town against slavery. Galesburg was an important station of the Underground Railroad, and its Presbyterian church withdrew from the presbytery in 1855 over the slavery condition of membership. The city was chartered in 1857. One of the Lincoln-Douglas debates was held on the Knox College grounds on the 7th of October 1858.
britannica-1911-goldberg:
Goldberg is a town of Germany, in the Prussian province of Silesia, 14 miles by rail south-west of Liegnitz, on the Katzbach. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 6,804 people in 1905. Its chief buildings are an old church from the early 13th century, an orphan institution of 1876, and a gymnasium founded in 1524 that once numbered Wallenstein among its pupils.

Woollen cloth, flannel, gloves, stockings, leather and beer are its manufactures, with a considerable trade in corn and fruit. The town owes its origin and name to a nearby gold mine, abandoned since the Hussite wars. It won civic rights in 1211 and suffered in turn from Tatars, plague, Hussites and the armies of the Thirty Years' War. Fighting near the town in May and August 1813 closes the entry. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Goldberg entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-greifenberg:
Greifenberg is a town of Germany, in the Prussian province of Pomerania, on the Rega, 45 miles north-east of Stettin on the Kolberg railway. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 7,208 people in 1905. It has two Evangelical churches, among them St Mary's, dating from the 13th century.

Two ancient gateways, a powder tower and a gymnasium complete the sights the entry names. Machine making, stoves and bricks are its principal industries. The town held municipal rights as early as 1262. In the 14th and 15th centuries it ran a considerable shipping trade. The Thirty Years' War cost it much of that prosperity, the entry says, and the short notice closes with a reference to Riemann's history of the town, published in 1862.
britannica-1911-hamann-johann-georg:
Johann Georg Hamann (1730–1788) was a German writer on philosophy and theology. He was born at Königsberg on 27 August 1730. His parents were humble and poor. His education was comprehensive but unsystematic. That want of order dogged his whole life. In 1746 he began theology, then deserted it for law. Law too was quickly relinquished. Reading and philology absorbed him instead.

Tutorships in Livonia and Courland both failed quickly. A Riga merchant, Johann Christoph Behrens, befriended him. They toured Germany, Holland and London together. Left in London, Hamann sank into extreme poverty. There he began earnest, prolonged study of the Bible. Deep pietism coloured his writing from that time. It also alienated many of his friends. He returned to Königsberg in 1759. His influence on the Sturm und Drang movement closes the account.
britannica-1911-hohenasperg:
Hohenasperg is an ancient fortress of Germany, in the kingdom of Württemberg, 10 m. N. of Stuttgart. It stands on a conical hill 1,100 ft. high, overlooking the town of Asperg. Once strongly fortified, it was long the state prison of Württemberg. It is now a reformatory.

Among the many held there were Joseph Süss-Oppenheimer, the Jewish financier (1692–1738), and the poet C. F. D. Schubart (1739–1791). The place belonged first to the counts of Calw, then to the counts palatine of Tübingen, and in 1308 it was acquired by Württemberg. Its fortifications were extended in 1535. In 1635 the Imperialists took the town and held it until 1649.
britannica-1911-hohenfriedberg:
Hohenfriedberg is a village of Silesia, about 6 m. from Striegau. It gives its name to a battle of the War of the Austrian Succession. It was fought on the 3rd of June 1745 between Frederick the Great's Prussians and the Austrians and Saxons under Prince Charles of Lorraine. In May 1745 Frederick drew his army together near Neisse, then moved north-west as the allies came toward the Elbe.

Frederick chose not to block the allies' passage from the mountains, but to fall on them as they came out. The allies, for their part, meant only to camp and cut him off from Breslau, sure he was at his wits' end. His army was in high spirits and eager for battle. By nine o'clock the battle was over and the allied army was fleeing to the mountains. Allied losses are given as 15,224 men, 72 guns and 83 standards; the Prussians lost 4,666 killed and wounded.
britannica-1911-hohenlimburg:
Hohenlimburg is a town of Germany, on the Lenne, in the Prussian province of Westphalia, 30 m. by rail S.E. of Dortmund. Its population was 12,790 in 1905. It has two Evangelical churches, a Roman Catholic church and a synagogue. Iron and metal industries centre there, and dyeing, cloth-making and linen-weaving are also carried on.

Hohenlimburg is the chief town of the county of Limburg and belonged of old to the counts of Limburg, whose family died out in 1508. It passed later to the counts of Bentheim-Tecklenburg. The castle of Hohenlimburg, which overlooks the town, is now the residence of Prince Adolf of Bentheim-Tecklenburg.
britannica-1911-hubertusburg: Hubertusburg is a château in the kingdom of Saxony, near the village of Wermsdorf, midway between Oschatz and Grimma. Frederick Augustus II, elector of Saxony and later King Augustus III of Poland, built it in 1721–1724 as a hunting box, often the scene of brilliant festivities. Its fame rests on the peace signed there on the 15th of February 1763, which ended the Seven Years' War. After many changes of use it now serves as a lunatic asylum and a training school for nursing sisters.
britannica-1911-kolberg:
Kolberg, also written Colberg, is a German seaport town in the Prussian province of Pomerania. It stands on the right bank of the Persante, about a mile above the point where the river reaches the Baltic. Railways join it to Belgard and Gollnow. In 1905 it held 22,804 people. Its market-place carries a statue of Frederick William III, and its great red-brick church of St Mary, with five aisles, dates from the 14th century.

The town has a harbour and lighthouse at the river mouth, makes woollen cloth, machinery and spirits, and draws many summer visitors to its bathing places. Kolberg began as a Slavonic fort, gained town rights in 1255 and joined the Hanseatic League in 1284. The Swedes took it in 1631, and it passed to Brandenburg at the peace of Westphalia. The Russians besieged it in vain in 1758 and 1760, then took it in 1762.
britannica-1911-kronenberg:
Kronenberg is a town of Germany in the Prussian Rhine Province. It lies 6 miles S.W. from Elberfeld, and is linked to that city by railway and by an electric tramway line. In 1905 it held 11,340 people. The town is a scattered place, made up of no fewer than seventy-three separate hamlets gathered under one name.

Kronenberg has a Roman Catholic church and two Protestant churches, along with a handsome modern town-hall. Its industries are of some size. They rest mainly on the making of steel and iron goods, the trades for which this part of the Rhine Province is known.
britannica-1911-kuttenberg:
Kuttenberg, in Czech Kutná Hora, is a town of Bohemia, in Austria, 45 miles E. by S. of Prague. In 1900 it held 14,799 people, most of them Czech. Its churches include the Gothic five-naved church of St Barbara, begun in 1368, the Gothic St Jacob of the 14th century, and the late Gothic Trinity church. The Wälscher Hof, once a royal house and mint, dates from the end of the 13th century.

The town grew from its silver mines, worked from the early 13th century. It rose fast, and by the Hussite troubles it stood next to Prague in Bohemia. Here Wenceslaus IV signed the decree of Kuttenberg on the 18th of January 1419, giving the Bohemian nation three votes at Prague University against one for the other three nations. That autumn the town's miners fell on Hussites and killed some 1600 people, many thrown alive into old mine shafts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-enge:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Engelberg describes a Benedictine house in Switzerland, dedicated to Our Lady of the Angels, at the head of the Nidwalden valley. Blessed Conrad, Count of Seldenburen, founded it in 1082. Its first abbot, Blessed Adelhelm of St. Blasien, received the founder himself as a monk.

Popes and emperors, beginning with Callistus the Second in 1124 and Henry the Fourth, granted the house wide rights. It stood directly under the Holy See until the Swiss Congregation formed in 1602. Engelberg's abbots held near-bishop power over their tenants and dependents, including the town that grew around the abbey walls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adolphus-von-:
Adolphus von Dalberg was Prince-Abbot of Fulda and founder of its university, born on 29 May 1678, who died on 3 November 1737 at Hammelburg. After serving as provost at Zelle in Hanover, he was elected Prince-Abbot of Fulda's Benedictine monastery in 1724. Though not a bishop, Dalberg held quasi-episcopal jurisdiction over abbey territory and held a diocesan synod in 1729.

Dalberg spared no pains to improve Fulda's Catholic education. Its once famous school, hurt in the sixteenth-century religious upheaval, had regained prestige through Jesuits and Benedictines. Hoping to restore the ancient seat of learning, he founded a university, the Alma Adolphina, joining Jesuit and Benedictine schools for philosophy and theology and adding law and medicine. Clement XII chartered it in 1732, Charles VI confirmed it in 1733, and it opened on 19 September 1733, lasting until 1805.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-bra:
Albert of Brandenburg was a cardinal and Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, born in June 1490 and dead in September 1545. By 1509 he held a prebend at Mainz cathedral, and he became Archbishop of Magdeburg in 1513, Archbishop of Mainz in 1514, and a cardinal in 1518. In 1517 he was charged with publishing in Saxony and Brandenburg the indulgence Pope Leo X had issued for building the new St. Peter's in Rome.

Martin Luther protested to Albert over the preaching of Tetzel and over Albert's book of instructions, but his letter was disregarded, and the entry calls the instructions wise and edifying. It paints the young bishop as worldly and extravagant, fond of learned men and artists. Yet it notes that he changed his conduct later in life. As a prince he ruled his electorate well, reforming justice, policing, and commerce, and he became a staunch defender of the Catholic faith in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augsburg:
Augsburg is a diocese in the Kingdom of Bavaria in Germany. Under the Archdiocese of Munich-Freising, it covers Swabia and Neuburg with parts of Upper Bavaria and Franconia. Its city appears in Strabo as Damasia, a stronghold of the Licatii. In 14 BC it became the Roman colony of Augusta Vindelicorum, soon prized as an arsenal and trade junction. Christianity likely reached it through soldiers or merchants, and a fourth-century community under Bishop Narcissus is linked to the martyrdom of St Afra.

The church there survived the fall of Roman power and the migrations, though little is certain before St Wikterp, bishop about 739 or 768. Later centuries brought splendor under St Ulrich, whose tomb stands in the Gothic church of St Ulrich and St Afra, built between 1467 and 1594. The entry closes with a survey of churches and abbeys across the diocese, many restored in baroque or rococo style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bamberg:
Bamberg is an archdiocese in Bavaria, covering most of Upper Franconia plus Nuremberg, Fürth, Ansbach, and Erlangen. Its province also holds the suffragan dioceses of Würzburg, Eichstätt, and Speyer. In 1900 it counted 379,442 Catholics, rising to 410,000 by 1907 against 720,000 of other faiths. Early on, Slavs peopled the region, and Fulda's Benedictine monks brought them Christianity under Würzburg's care.

Emperor Henry II and his wife Kunigunde chose to erect a separate bishopric at Bamberg, a family inheritance. Their aims were to shrink unwieldy Würzburg and to root Christianity firmer in Franconia. After long talks with Würzburg and Eichstätt, the boundaries were set in 1008, with papal confirmation that year. The new cathedral was consecrated on 6 May 1012, and in 1017 Henry founded a Benedictine abbey for training clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-joseph-:
Baron Joseph Maria Christoph von Lassberg was a distinguished German antiquary, born at Donaueschingen in 1770, who died in 1855. His father was chief forester to Prince von Fürstenberg, and Lassberg served the prince from 1789, becoming chief forest warden in 1804. As privy councillor from 1806, he traveled Switzerland, Italy, and England with the regent Princess Elizabeth. Retiring in 1817, he lived at Eppishusen, then from 1838 at Castle Meersburg on Lake Constance.

There he devoted himself to German literature, gathering over 12,000 books and 273 manuscripts, including the Hohenems Nibelungenlied codex. After his death the library went to Donaueschingen, and his guests at Meersburg included Uhland, Lachmann, and Schwab. Editing medieval German poems under the name Meister Sepp von Eppishusen, he published the four-volume Liedersaal at St Gall. Its fourth volume first printed the Nibelungen manuscript he owned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-lu: Bernard of Luxemburg, a Dominican theologian and inquisitor, was born at Strassen near Cologne and died at Cologne in 1535. He studied at Cologne, took a degree at Louvain in 1499, and served as prior of Cologne twice. As inquisitor for Cologne, Mainz, and Trier, he defended Catholic teaching against heretics, though his Catalogue of Heretics shows weak critical judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernhard-hein:
Bernhard Heinrich Overberg, a German priest and educator, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born poor at Höckel near Osnabrück in 1754, he died in 1826 after rising from pedlar's son to school reformer. A priest prepared him for college at fifteen, and he studied with the Franciscans at Rheine and at Münster, where he was ordained in 1779.

Good work teaching religion at Everswinkel won him the directorship of Münster's new normal school, a school for training teachers, under Fürstenberg. He trained women teachers in particular, effectively creating the lay woman teacher in Germany, and taught catechism free for twenty-seven years. The entry presents a humble founder of modern teacher training.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berthold-of-h:
Berthold of Henneberg, Archbishop and Elector of Mainz, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1441, he died in 1504 after study at Erfurt and a canonry at Cologne in 1464. Court service under Emperor Frederick III followed, and he was chosen Archbishop of Mainz in 1484.

As imperial chancellor he won the right to countersign royal documents when Maximilian was elected king in 1486. Heart and soul for reform of the tottering empire, he pressed for a new constitution, a common tax, and a supreme court. The entry presents a prince-bishop who tried to give Germany order before the Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-gertrude-o: Blessed Gertrude of Aldenberg, Premonstratensian abbess, was born about 1227, youngest daughter of Louis VI of Thuringia and St. Elizabeth of Hungary. Her father died travelling toward the Holy Land before her birth, and Elizabeth brought the two-year-old to Aldenberg convent, where Gertrude became a nun. Elected abbess at twenty-one in 1248, she ruled forty-nine years, using her uncle's inheritance for the house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brandenburg:
Brandenburg, once an electoral Mark and diocese in Prussia's heart, grew from Slavic lands east of the Elbe won back by German kings. Slav tribes pushed to the Elbe and Saale in the sixth century until Charlemagne checked them. Henry I seized Brennabor and founded the North Mark, and Otto I set up Havelberg and Brandenburg dioceses in 948 under Magdeburg.

A Slav rising in 983 retook both sees and wiped out the young Christian order. Real evangelization waited for Albert of Ballenstadt, made Margrave in 1134, who befriended Prince Pribislav, inherited Brandenburg in 1150, and brought Rhine colonists to drain its swamps. Premonstratensians and Cistercians led the conversion, refounding dioceses, churches, and monasteries, and winning the Wends to church and empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-centuriators-:
The Centuriators of Magdeburg were a group of Lutheran scholars who gathered at Magdeburg and produced a church history arranged century by century. In 1559 the first three folio volumes appeared at Basle under the title Ecclesiastica Historia, a church history by some learned and pious men of Magdeburg. The name Centuriators stuck because of their century-by-century division and the place where the first five volumes were written. Most later volumes were written at Wismar or elsewhere.

The originator and moving spirit was Matthias Vlacich, latinized Flacius and called Illyricus from his native Istria. Born in 1520, he was kept from becoming a monk by his uncle Baldo Lupertino, an apostate friar. He went to Germany in 1539, studying at Augsburg, Basle, Tübingen, and Wittenberg. The Augsburg Interim of 1547 drew him into the Adiaphoristic controversy, in which he attacked Philip Melanchthon bitterly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-etien:
Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg was born at Bourbourg in France in 1814 and died at Nice in 1874. He left France for Canada in 1845, and in 1846 served as vicar-general at Boston. After two winters in Rome searching archives for Spanish American documents, he went to Mexico in 1848 as chaplain of the French Legation. From 1854 he travelled through Central America, reaching Guatemala City in February 1855 and administering the Rabinal district in Vera Paz for a year.

He returned to France in 1857, revisited Tehuantepec, Chiapas, and Guatemala in 1859 and 1860, and joined the French scientific mission to Mexico in 1864. His publications from 1857 to 1871 remain valuable, though the entry warns that early enthusiasm and vivid fancy flawed them. Exhausted by long, arduous, and often dangerous labours, he died at Nice aged sixty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-leo:
Michael Ott's entry follows Conrad of Leonberg, called Leontorius, Cistercian monk and humanist born at Leonberg in 1460, died at Engenthal near Basle after 1520. He took vows at Maulbronn, then enjoying a golden age unlike most Cistercian houses. In 1490 he became his order's general's secretary. As German humanists revived Latin and Greek classics, Conrad, deploring barbarous scholastic Latin, joined their push to restore Ciceronian Latinity.

By word and example he encouraged Greek study, but Reuchlin, Hebrew scholar who died in 1522, drew him most, inspiring his Hebrew enthusiasm. Like Reuchlin, friend and teacher, Conrad held Hebrew necessary for Scripture and ranked among the few great Hebrew scholars of his time. He corresponded with leading writers, highly esteemed by learned men. For a time he proofread at Amerbach's Basle press. Beyond Latin poems, orations, and epistles, he published at Basle in 1506 to 1508 a Latin Bible with Lyra, Burgos, and Thoring additions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-mar:
Johann Peter Kirsch's entry follows Conrad of Marburg, confessor of Saint Elizabeth of Thuringia and papal inquisitor. Born at or near Marburg late in the twelfth century, he died on 30 July 1233. Men of his day called him Magister, proof of a finished course, perhaps at Paris or Bologna. Berthold and Caesarius of Heisterbach mark him likely a secular priest, neither Dominican as Hausrath states nor Franciscan as Henke asserts.

Papal letters and writers of his day credit him with skill, learning, speech gifts, zeal for the faith, and a stern life. He first appears preaching Innocent III's crusade of 1213 with vigor. In 1225, after Rodeger's recall, he became the landgravine's guide and confessor. Even friendly writers found his rule too severe and harsh. First inquisitor named in Germany, he was killed returning to Marburg, and his successor sought harsh justice for his killers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-bonifa:
A biographical entry presents Daniel Bonifacius von Haneberg, a German prelate and Orientalist born near Kempten in 1816 and dead at Speyer in 1876. At Kempten he mastered Hebrew, Arabic, Syriac, Persian, and Ethiopic with hardly any guidance, then at Munich added Sanskrit and Chinese while studying philosophy and theology. Ordained at Augsburg in 1839, he took a doctorate at Munich the same year.

His thirty-three years lecturing on the Old Testament at Munich made him extraordinary professor of Hebrew in 1841 and ordinary professor in 1844, his learning, discretion, and piety drawing growing audiences. Later he became Bishop of Speyer, touring his diocese until pneumonia, caught on a visitation, ended his life. Clergy and people revered him as a saint, and the entry lists his works and biographers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-of-augs:
A biographical entry follows David of Augsburg, a medieval German mystic born probably at Augsburg early in the thirteenth century and dead there on 19 November 1272. Joining the Franciscans probably at Ratisbon, he served as master of novices and wrote his celebrated Formula Novitiorum for their spiritual benefit. In 1246 he and Berthold of Ratisbon inspected the convent of Niedermunster.

From about 1250 David accompanied Berthold on missionary tours, likely preaching himself, and shared in Inquisition proceedings against the Waldenses. Legend says Berthold, preaching far away on David's death day, broke off to quote a hymn for his departed friend. David wrote in Latin and German, and his Latin works were long misattributed to Bernard and Bonaventure, proof of the esteem they commanded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diether-of-is:
Diether of Isenburg was Archbishop and Elector of Mainz, born about 1412. He studied at Erfurt, where he became rector in 1434, and held canonries at Mainz, Cologne, and Trier while still young. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he sought the see of Trier in 1456 and failed. Three years later he won election to Mainz itself, likely through simony, the buying of church office.

His reign brought the Mainz feud of 1461 to 1463, a bitter quarrel over the archbishopric that drew in princes and popes. The entry follows his quarrels, his deposition, and his later return to power. He died at Aschaffenburg in 1482, a prince of the church whose ambition shaped German politics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-friedri:
Franz Friedrich Wilhelm von Furstenberg, born at Herdringen in Westphalia on 7 August 1729 and dead at Munster on 16 September 1810. He was a statesman and educator who rebuilt Munster's schools and government. Tutored privately and by Jesuits at Cologne, he studied law at Cologne, Salzburg, and the Sapienza in Rome, became canon of Munster in 1748 and of Paderborn. He took minor orders without intending priesthood. During the Seven Years' War he served his country as go-between for opposing camps, warding off many calamities from Munster.

After Clemens August died in 1761, Furstenberg's influence secured Maximilian Friedrich as Prince-Bishop of Munster in 1762. The new ruler entrusted him with temporal and spiritual administration, making him privy councillor and minister in 1762 and vicar-general and curator of schools in 1770. Prussian rule after 1803 eroded his power, and he resigned in 1807.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-wilhelm:
Franz Wilhelm, Count von Wartenberg, eldest son of Duke Ferdinand of Bavaria and his morganatic wife Maria Pettenbeckin, was born at Munich on 1 March 1593. He died at Ratisbon on 1 December 1661. He was a bishop and cardinal of the Counter-Reformation. Elected Bishop of Osnabruck on 26 October 1625, he found the faith there in deplorable state, its three previous bishops Protestant.

With Tilly's help he took possession of his see on 12 March 1628, driving out Danish soldiers. Then he pursued Counter-Reformation with zeal: expelling Protestant preachers, restoring churches to Catholics, purging the city council, taking education in hand. He gave the former Augustinian convent to Jesuits as teachers at the Gymnasium Carolinum, restored and founded religious communities, and held synods to enforce Trent's decrees. Driven out by war and the Peace of Westphalia, he kept spiritual jurisdiction, regained Osnabruck on 18 December 1650, and was made cardinal-priest on 5 April 1661.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-freiburg:
Freiburg, a city in Baden at the foot of the Black Forest, anchors a Catholic Encyclopedia entry that covers city, archdiocese, and university together. Founded in 1120 by Conrad of Zähringen, it grew as a market town on both banks of the Dreisam. By the census of December 1905 it held 76,286 people, of whom 53,133 were Catholics.

The city bought its liberties from cash-strapped lords and placed itself under Austria in 1368, sharing Habsburg fortunes for five centuries. Its minster rose from the twelfth century onward, and Archduke Albert founded its university in 1456. Dominicans, Franciscans, and mystics all left marks here, from Albert the Great to Berthold the Black, the friar linked in legend with gunpowder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-pri:
Friedrich of Schwarzenberg, cardinal and prince-archbishop of Prague, was born at Vienna in April 1809 into a princely house touched early by tragedy. When he was a month old his mother fled Napoleon with him to Bohemia. A year later she died with her eldest daughter in a fire at Paris festivities, known only by a gold necklace engraved with her ten children's names.

Raised by his aunt, young Fritz studied law, then told his father he wished to serve God as a priest. He studied theology at Salzburg and Vienna, took his doctorate, and was ordained in 1833. As a cathedral curate he loved parish work, and his rise to Prague's highest see crowned a career shaped by pastoral care and loyalty to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerhoh-of-rei:
Gerhoh of Reichersberg, provost and Austin canon, ranked among twelfth-century Germany's finest theologians. Born at Polling, Bavaria, in 1093, he studied at Freising, Mosburg, and Hildesheim, and in 1119 Bishop Hermann of Augsburg made him scholasticus and canon. Adopting a stricter church line, he quit the simoniacal Hermann in 1121 for Raitenbuch monastery, returning with him to the Lateran Council of 1123.

Gerhoh joined Raitenbuch's Austin canons in 1124 with his father and half-brothers, was ordained in 1126, and held Cham parish until Hohenstaufen threats drove him out in 1127. Salzburg's Conrad made him Reichersberg's provost in 1132, sending him often to Rome and, in 1143, to Bohemia and Moravia with Arnold of Brescia. In the disputed election of 1159 he backed Alexander III after long hesitation. He endured imperial hatred, banishment of his archbishop in 1166, and attacks on his monastery before dying on his return in 1169. His writings press Gregorian reform of the clergy through community life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gottfried-von:
Gottfried von Strasburg was one of the greatest of Middle High German epic poets, about whose life nothing is known. Even his poem gives no information, and his birth and death dates cannot be fixed. A Catholic Encyclopedia article dates his Tristan und Isolt about 1210 from an internal clue.

In the eighth book, Hartmann and Wolfram appear as still living, while Reinmar of Hagenau and Heinrich von Veldeke are spoken of as dead. Called Meister rather than Herr, he may have been a burgher, though the title can denote learning, and he certainly knew Latin and French and courtly life. His Tristan, sent by King Marke to woo Isolde, tells how the pair mistakenly drink a love potion. They fall madly in love, until Tristan flees and the poem breaks off.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-graf-von-fran:
Johann Heinrich, Graf von Frankenberg, was Archbishop of Mechlin, Primate of Belgium, and cardinal, born on 18 September 1726 at Gross-Glogau in Silesia, who died at Breda on 11 June 1804. Sole male heir of a family devoted to the Habsburgs, he chose the priesthood young. He studied at Breslau and the German College at Rome, and was ordained in 1749. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a life of every private and public virtue.

Made coadjutor of Görz in 1750 and dean at Prague in 1754, he became Archbishop of Mechlin in 1759. He defended his office's dignity against Austrian ministers who sought Lenten dispensations at their pleasure and meddled in ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Maria Theresa favored him and sought his cardinal's hat in 1778, but Joseph II's Josephinism, the absolute supremacy of the state, changed the situation entirely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-of-he:
Gregory of Heimburg was a humanist and statesman born at Wurzburg in the beginning of the fifteenth century, who died at Tharandt near Dresden in August 1472. About 1430 he took the degree of Doctor of Both Laws at Padua, and, filled with reform ideas, was drawn to the Council of Basle. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an ardent and eloquent jurist.

At Basle he became secretary to Aeneas Sylvius. He left in 1433 when elected syndic of Nuremberg, and served in that office until 1461. He headed embassies to Eugene IV in 1446 over the deposed archbishops of Cologne and Trier, but his mission failed, and the Concordat of Vienna followed in 1448. Disappointed even by neutrality, he abandoned ecclesiastical politics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hamburg:
Hamburg's church story begins with a fishing settlement between Elbe and Alster, fortified by Charlemagne about 805. Louis the Pious raised it in 831 into an archbishopric for all northern missions, under St. Ansgar, Apostle of the North. Driven by Northmen to Bremen, Ansgar joined the two sees, a union Nicholas I ratified in 864. His successors Rimbert and Unni carried the gospel into Denmark and Sweden.

Under Adalbert the Great the see reached its height and its troubles, chronicled by Adam of Bremen. It then sank as Lund became the northern metropolis and the see moved to Bremen in 1223. Commerce and the Hanseatic League then eclipsed church power. The Reformation, welcomed eagerly in 1525, drove the Catholic clergy out by 1528, with the last public Mass in 1529.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harrisburg:
Pennsylvania's Diocese of Harrisburg, established in 1868 from Philadelphia, covers fifteen counties across 8,000 square miles, after Lycoming and Centre went to Altoona in 1901. At its founding some 25,000 Catholics were served by only about twenty priests and as many churches, in a poor farming and mining country.

Jeremiah F. Shanahan, its first bishop, led it slowly from 1868 to 1886, Thomas McGovern followed to 1898, by which time churches had grown to fifty and priests to fifty-five. John Walter Shanahan, the first bishop's brother, took office in 1899. Present figures count 86 priests, 63 churches with resident priests, 36 parish schools with 8,000 pupils, and 57,000 Catholics, including Poles, Slavs, Italians, Greeks, and Lithuanians in the mines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-von-:
Fifteenth-century German poet Heinrich von Laufenberg, a Freiburg priest and later cathedral dean who entered the Knights of St. John in 1445, wrote sermons, verse renderings, and the religious lyrics that secure his fame. His rhymed German Mirror of Human Salvation of 1437 tells Fall and Redemption with Bible stories read as symbols, and a second long rendering glorifies Mary through Old Testament tales.

Both long works were lost when Strasbourg was besieged in 1870, but a metrical German version of a health treatise from 1429 survives. His lyrics matter most: renderings of Latin hymns, original songs of love for Jesus and Mary, and contrafacta that keep folk tunes and diction while pouring a religious spirit into them. Acrostics and artifice mar some original pieces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herrad-of-lan:
Herrad of Landsberg was a twelfth-century abbess and author of the Hortus Deliciarum, or Garden of Delights. Born about 1130 to a noble Alsatian family, she entered the convent of Hohenburg in the Vosges at an early age. She became abbess in 1167 and held office until her death in 1195. She began her great work in 1165, within the cloister walls.

The text gathers the sciences studied in her day, including theology, into a compendium meant for the novices of her house. It shows wide reading rather than high originality, and it gives a clear picture of education in twelfth-century cloister schools. Its chief glory lies in its 336 illustrations, many of them symbolic scenes, historical pictures, and portraits of her sisters in religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hohenburg:
Hohenburg, also called Odilienberg or Altitona, was a suppressed nunnery on the most famous of the Vosges mountains in Alsace. St. Odilia founded it about 690 and served as its first abbess. On the eastern slope she built a hospice called Niedermünster, later a convent for ladies of nobility, which lightning destroyed in 1572.

Benedictine nuns first held the house, replaced by canonesses in the eleventh century. Discipline faded, but Abbess Relindis restored it about 1140, and the house grew famed for strict life and learned nuns. Her successor Herrad von Landsperg, abbess from 1167, built two more monasteries on the mountain and wrote the Hortus Deliciarum, a treasury of theology, astronomy, and philosophy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-stras:
Hugh of Strasburg was a theologian of the later thirteenth century, whose birth and death dates are unknown. His fame rests on the Compendium of Theology, or Compendium of Theological Truth, now judged to be his work. For four hundred years it served as a textbook, thanks to its scope, style, and practical arrangement, and it was copied and printed again and again.

The work runs to seven books treating the last four things, grace, the sacraments, the incarnation, the fall, and creation. Few medieval works have been ascribed to so many authors: early printed editions name no author, some name Ulrich of Strasburg, and one index-maker, Thomas Dorinberg, was long mistaken for the author. Recent research has settled the question in Hugh's favour, the entry argues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignaz-heinric:
Ignaz Heinrich von Wessenberg was vicar-general and administrator of Constance, born at Dresden in 1774 and dead at Constance in 1860. He studied at Augsburg, Dillingen, Würzburg, and Vienna. By eighteen he already held canonries at Constance, Augsburg, and Basle, and in 1802, still a subdeacon, he became vicar-general for Prince-Primate Dalberg's Constance diocese. Only in 1812, at thirty-eight, did he take priest's orders.

Wessenberg was, the entry judges, entirely unfit for the post. Wide knowledge notwithstanding, profound scholarship eluded him, and his theological training fell far short. Josephinist and Febronian principles, absorbed in youth, led him to advocate a German national church loosely tied to Rome, state-supported and shielded against papal interference. He aired those views in his 1801 Spirit of the Age and in a monthly review he founded in 1802.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-geiler:
Johann Geiler von Kayserberg, a celebrated German pulpit orator born at Schaffhausen in 1445 and dead at Strasbourg in 1510. He preached to common people at the turn of the sixteenth century. His surname came from Kayserberg, where the grandfather who raised him lived after his father was killed hunting.

Geiler, a secular priest like his friend Wimpheling, educator of Germany, fought church abuses not as Luther would, but by restoring Christian morals in church and state under church doctrine. Where Wimpheling's field was the school, Geiler's was the pulpit, and literary history can fix his place exactly: a voice linking Strasbourg humanists to ordinary hearers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-gutenb:
Johann Gutenberg, inventor of printing with movable type, was born about 1400 at Mainz and died there in 1467 or 1468. Properly Henne Gänsfleisch zur Laden, he took Gutenberg from his father's house, and his patrician family, traced to the thirteenth century, served as retainers of the archbishop's mint.

That mint connection likely gave Gutenberg metal skill: his kin supplied coin metal, changed coin kinds, and sat on forgery trials. His father Friele married Else Wyrich in 1386 and died in 1419. Of Johann's youth little is known, save that he was away from Mainz in 1418, His press, built on mint craft and goldsmith work, remade how books reached the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-michae:
Johann Michael Nathanael Feneberg was a Bavarian priest whose parish work at Seeg drew him into suspicion of false mysticism. Born in 1751, he studied at Kaufbeuren and Augsburg, joined the Jesuits in 1770, and was ordained in 1775 after the order was suppressed. He taught at Dillingen, lost his post amid charges of leaning toward the Illuminati, and became pastor of Seeg, where he mapped its villages and took a census of the district.

A fall from his horse cost him a leg, which he bore without an anesthetic. His friendship with the preacher Martin Boos then pulled him into trouble: Boos's followers, called the Awakened Brethren, called Feneberg Nathanael. Church officials seized his papers in 1797 and investigated him and his assistants, and the entry traces how that inquiry shadowed the rest of his pastoral life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-falke:
John of Falkenberg was a Dominican master of theology whose violent book for the Teutonic Knights made him a byword of the Council of Constance. Born at Falkenberg in Pomerania, he spent his novitiate at Kammin and taught philosophy and theology for years. In the papal schism he backed the legitimate Gregory XII against his order's general and brethren, who favored the antipopes. He publicly refused at Constance to acknowledge his superior.

In the Teutonic Order's war with Poland and Lithuania he wrote that King Wladislaw and his adherents were idolaters and unbelievers. He held that war against them was noble and, following Jean Petit, that killing the Polish king was lawful. His Tres tractatuli defended that position against Gerson and the Paris doctors, denying bishops the right to condemn his book. Imprisoned by the Archbishop of Gnesen, he died about 1418.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-edmund:
Joseph Edmund Jörg was a Bavarian historian, journalist, and politician who lived from 1819 to 1901. The son of a junior official, he studied theology, then switched to philology and history at Munich with Döllinger. In 1852 he joined the Bavarian Record Office and took over the Historisch-politische Blätter, which he edited for decades.

Jörg wrote on the German Peasants' War, on Protestantism, and, as early as 1867, on socialist parties. A conservative Bavarian monarchist, he sat in the Bavarian Lower House until 1881 and in the German Reichstag from 1874 to 1879. He fought Prussian dominance and helped build the Bavarian People's Party into a House majority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kaspar-ulenbe:
Kaspar Ulenberg (1549-1617) grew up Lutheran in Westphalia, trained for the Lutheran ministry at Wittenberg, and then crossed to the Catholic Church in 1572. This entry follows a career that carried him from parish work in Kaiserswerth and Cologne to the rectorship of Cologne University.

Doubts raised by reading Luther and by quarrels among Protestant divines, plus friendship with Catholics in Cologne, drove the change. Once ordained, he preached, taught catechism classes, and won many converts, while directing the Laurentian school for twenty-two years and tutoring two Baden princes. His books include a popular hymn collection of the Psalms, a defence of the old faith, and a German Bible translation that kept his name alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-konrad-of-meg:
Konrad of Megenberg (1309-1374) was a prolific fourteenth-century German scholar, born near Schweinfurt, trained at Erfurt and Paris, head of St. Stephen's school at Vienna in 1337, and parish priest, canon, and councillor at Ratisbon from 1342.

His best-known book, Buch der Natur, written in 1349, surveys all then known of natural history and stands as the first natural history in German. Freely reworked from Thomas of Cantimpre's Latin work, with omissions, corrections, and his own observations, it was widely read into the sixteenth century and first printed at Augsburg in 1475. His other writings range from astronomy and morals to a poem lamenting the Church in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-konrad-of-wur:
Konrad of Wurzburg (about 1230-1287) was the leading Middle High German story-poet after the three great masters of epic, modelling himself on Gottfried von Strassburg. A burgher by rank, he bears the title Meister, and lived mostly at Strasburg and Basle.

His output spans verse romances, love songs, and sayings. The Schwanritter retells the Lohengrin tale without the Grail, and shorter pieces include Otto with the Beard and the famous Tale of a Heart. Longer works from French sources include Partonopier, about the knight Partonopeus and the fairy Meliur, and a Trojan War epic of over 50,000 verses. His religious verse crowns the Virgin in The Golden Forge, where the poet works as a smith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lemberg:
Lemberg, Polish Lwow and Latin Leopol, seats a Latin, a Uniat Ruthenian, and a Uniat Armenian archbishopric. Ruthenian King Daniel founded it in 1259 for his son Leo, Prince of Halicz, whose name it took, though Tatars destroyed it in 1261 and Leo rebuilt it in 1270.

Casimir the Great took it in 1340, built two castles, drew German colonists, and chartered it on Magdeburg's model. Louis of Hungary, Hedwig's dowry, and Jagellon's marriage made it Poland's capital of Red Russia, autonomous until 1433, and a great entrepot of Europe's eastern trade after Constantinople fell. Sieges by Lithuanians, Wallachians, Turks, and Cossacks, Charles XII's sack in 1704, Austria's gain in 1772, and the 1848 revolt and bombardment mark its later story. In a deep Pelter valley it holds about 160,000 people, 45,000 of them Jews.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-limburg:
Limburg, in the Kingdom of Prussia, is a diocese suffragan of Freiburg, dating from the end of the eighteenth century.

When Coblenz fell to the French in 1794, Archdeacon Joseph Ludwig Beck was given jurisdiction over Trier's right-bank diocese. When the left bank passed to France in 1801, three rural deaneries on the right bank continued. In 1803 they passed to Nassau-Weilburg's princes, who kept the Limburg vicariate-general going, diverted church revenues, and suppressed the city's collegiate chapter. In 1802 Trier's last archbishop, Klemens Wenceslaus, named Beck sole vicar-general of the archdiocese's remnant, and after the archbishop's death in 1812 the pope confirmed Beck in 1813. The primate Dalberg then named Hubert Anton Corden, pastor of Limburg, administrator of the vicariate. Pius VII named him vicar Apostolic for Trier's archdiocese on 8 July 1818.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-guillau:
Louis Guillaume Valentin Dubourg was second Bishop of Louisiana and the Floridas, later Archbishop of Besancon, born in Santo Domingo in 1766 and dead at Besancon in 1833. Ordained at Paris in 1788, he fled the Revolution to America in 1794 and led Georgetown College from 1796 to 1799.

As administrator of Louisiana from 1812, he tamed a unruly diocese and greeted General Jackson with victory laurels at New Orleans cathedral in 1815. Consecrated bishop that year, he founded a seminary and college at the Barrens and the St. Louis Latin Academy, seed of St. Louis University. He returned to France in 1826, first to Montauban, then to Besancon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-maimbou:
Louis Maimbourg was a French church historian, born at Nancy in 1610 and dead at Paris in 1686. He joined the Jesuits in 1626, taught rhetoric and humanities for six years, and won fame as a preacher before turning to history.

Prolific and elegant, he wrote against Jansenism and Protestantism and defended Gallican liberties, the French church's freedoms, against Rome. That defence cost him his place: Innocent XI ordered his expulsion from the Society in 1681. Louis XIV gave him a pension, and he wrote on at St. Victor until his death, though critics judge his graceful histories shaky, and several landed on the Index.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luxemburg:
Luxemburg is a small neutral grand duchy, independent since 11 May 1867, covering 998 square miles between Belgium, Prussia, Lorraine, and France. Wooded and watered by Moselle, Sure, Our, and Alzette, it lies about a thousand feet up, grows grain, feeds cattle and horses, and presses over 1,300,000 gallons of wine a year.

Iron ore beds of 10,000 acres drive its industry. Roads and railways knit its 250,000 people, nearly all Germanic, speaking a Palatinate-like dialect, with French in law and High German in church and school. Almost all are Catholic, with barely 3,000 Protestants and 1,200 Jews, and their own bishop since 1870, after centuries under Trier, Liege, Metz, and Namur.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magdeburg:
Magdeburg stood on the Elbe as capital of the Prussian province of Saxony. It was a busy trading city, known above all for sugar making. Its people numbered about 241,000. From 968 to 1552 it was the seat of an archbishopric. That long church role shaped its standing among German towns.

Trade with the Wends across the river made it an old German market centre. The Reformation found quick support there. Luther had once been a schoolboy in the town. Later, secular princes replaced archbishops as administrators. War in the seventeenth century battered the city, and blame for a great fire stayed disputed. A second half traces the archbishopric, its small diocese, and its slow change under princely rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marienberg:
Marienberg was a Benedictine abbey of the St Joseph Congregation near Mals in Tyrol. Its founding reaches back to Charlemagne, who set up a monastery near Taufers between 780 and 786. Two centuries on, Eberhard of Tarasp built Schuls in the Engadine for the men, consecrated in 1078 or 1079.

After lightning wrecked Schuls, it was rebuilt and consecrated in 1131. Ulrich IV of Tarasp brought Ottobeuern monks to revive it and raised the priory to an abbey. He moved the community to St Stephen in 1146 and to the hill near Burgeis in 1150, where Marienberg has stood since. Later trials included sack under Abbot Konrad III, murder of Abbot Hermann in 1304, and plague in 1348, sparing only the abbot, a priest, a lay brother, and Goswin, its chronicler. Fires in 1418 and 1656, decline, reform under Abbot Mathias Lang, dissolution by Bavaria in 1807, and restoration by Francis II in 1816 fill its later story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martinsberg:
Martinsberg, or Pannonhalma, was an important Benedictine abbey in Hungary, fourteen miles south of Raab and sixty west of Buda-Pesth. Long held as St Martin of Tours's birthplace and early home, it drew great veneration from Hungary's small Christian population. Duke Geysa began the monastery late in the tenth century, and his son St Stephen the king completed it, dedicating its church on the second Sunday of October 1001.

Its fortunes varied across centuries of war and reform. An eclipse of about sixteen years ended on 12 March 1802, when abbey and colleges reopened at the nation's general desire under Archabbot Chrysostom Novak. Since then the community has prospered, abbey and church rebuilt in Italian style as an imposing group. The archabbot, a prelate nullius subject at once to the Holy See, heads the Hungarian Benedictine congregation and sits in the House of Magnates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-of-n:
The Latin chronicle long tied to Albert of Strasburg is now generally credited to Matthias of Neuburg. He was a chronicler born near the close of the thirteenth century, perhaps at Neuburg in Baden. He died between 1364 and 1370, likely at Strasburg. He studied law at Bologna and took minor orders without becoming a priest. In 1327 he served as solicitor of the Basle episcopal court, and later as clerk to Bishop Berthold von Buchecke at Strasburg.

His chronicle covers 1243 to 1350, with a first continuation to 1355, and later writers carried it to 1368, 1374, and 1378. It matters most for Alsatian and Habsburg history. Its pages for 1346-1350 rank among the best sources for the whole empire in those years. The entry also traces the long dispute over authorship, once argued for Jacob of Mainz and Albert of Strasburg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-von-:
Matthias von Schoenberg, a German Jesuit author born at Ehingen in 1732, wrote for ordinary readers as much as for scholars. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1750. From 1766 to 1772 he ran the Eleemosyna Aurea, a project that spread instructive books in a style even the unlettered could follow. After the Society's suppression, Bavaria's elector made him his church councillor.

An untiring defender of Christian morals and the Catholic faith, Schoenberg compiled prayer books and edited school works. He wrote treatises on the basic truths of religion plus many devotional books that stirred love for Mary and the Sacred Heart. Nearly forty of his writings ran through five and six editions. His best-known titles include Die Zierde der Jugend and Der hofliche Schuler. He died at Munich in 1792.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mechtild-of-m:
Mechtild of Magdeburg, a famed medieval mystic born of Saxon nobility about 1210, died at the Cistercian nunnery of Helfta near Eisleben about 1285. She felt her first inspirations at twelve, when, by her own account, the Holy Ghost greeted her. From then on the greeting came daily. Longing to be despised though undeserving it, she left a loving home to become a Beguine at Magdeburg in 1230.

Under Dominican guidance she lived in prayer and harsh self-denial. Her visions grew so frequent and striking that her confessor ceased to doubt their divine source. At his order she reluctantly wrote them down. After 1270 she joined the Cistercian nuns at Helfta, spending her last twelve years honoured as one specially favoured by God, above all by her namesake St. Mechtilde of Hackeborn and St. Gertrude the Great. Her book, the Flowing Light of the Godhead, records her visions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mecklenburg:
Mecklenburg, a division of the German Empire, holds the two grand duchies of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz. At the dawn of the Christian era Germanic tribes lived there, but by the second century they began to leave, and Slavonic tribes poured in. By about 600 the Slavs held the land entire, chiefly Wends: Obotrites west and Lusici, or Wilzen, east. They lived by forestry, cattle, hunting, and fishing, and worshipped nature.

Their chief god was Radegast Zuarasici, whose shrine at Rethra served all Mecklenburg until its ruin in the twelfth century. Svantevit, the holy oracle at Arkona on Rugen, then took his place. After Charlemagne tamed the Saxons, Mecklenburg bordered the Frankish Empire and traded briskly, Bardowiek leading as Slav mart under the Saxon emperors. Henry I forced tribute about 928 and set Saxon counts over the land, opening the road by which Christianity entered with German rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-of-s:
Nicholas of Strasburg, a mystic flourishing early in the fourteenth century, was educated at Paris and later lector at Cologne's Dominican convent. John XXII appointed him to inspect the German Dominican province, where bitter discord reigned.
