Relying on two papal briefs of 1 August 1325, his sole commission was reforming the province in head and members and acting as visitor to the sisters.

Nicholas also assumed the inquisitor's office, closing a process Archbishop Heinrich of Cologne had begun against Master Eckhart over mysticism, in Eckhart's favour in 1326. In January 1327 the archbishop reopened the case and accused Nicholas of shielding his brother friar's errors. Almost at once, Hermann von Hochst, a discontented religious Nicholas had justly penalised, had him excommunicated. Pope John soon released him to serve as definitor at Perpignan's general chapter on 31 May 1327. He was last heard of as vicar of the German Dominicans in 1329.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nuremberg:
Nuremberg, Bavaria's second city on the Pegnitz, grew from an imperial castle town into a free city of diets, crafts, and reform. First named Noremberc under Henry III, it gained fair and mint rights in 1062, freedom from tolls in 1112, and splendid castles under Barbarossa.

Emperors sheltered there in war, diets met within its walls, and its patron Saint Sebald drew pilgrims, while Jews found asylum under Conrad III. The entry carries the city through Hohenstaufen and burgrave rule, its crafts and printing, and the Reformation that divided its churches. Several diets met there under Frederick Barbarossa, builder of a splendid new imperial castle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ogdensburg:
Ogdensburg, a New York diocese covering the northern counties from the Adirondacks to Lake Ontario, spans 12,036 square miles of forest, rock, and sand. Its land once saw Iroquois wars and French-British fighting, and Sulpician Francis Picquet built the Fort of the Presentation there in 1749 for Christian Mohawks.

Scattered by the English a decade later, those Mohawks survive at Saint Regis, split between Canada and New York. The entry records the diocese's parishes, its summer resorts and tuberculosis sanatoria, and a rural population slowly shifting to iron-mining towns. A reservation called Saint Regis still holds descendants of the Christianized tribes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oldenburg:
Oldenburg, a grand duchy of the German Empire, yoked three far-flung lands: Oldenburg proper, Lübeck, and Birkenfeld. Together they covered 2,571 square miles and held 438,856 people in 1905, with Catholics at 96,067 against nearly 400,000 Protestants.

Frisian in the coastal north and Low Saxon inland, the duchy lived by farming, shipping, and trade, and its Catholic minority, 21.9 percent against 22.4 in 1871, shrank as farm folk left for factory districts. The entry maps its parishes, schools, and church life. Its capital is Oldenburg, and its coastal people are of Frisian descent. Inland the population is Low Saxon, while Frisians live along the North Sea coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otfried-of-we:
Otfried of Weissenburg stands as the earliest named German poet, writer of the Evangelienbuch, the Gospels retold in rhyme. He flourished in the ninth century, though his exact dates are unknown. Probably born near Weissenburg in Alsace, he studied at Fulda under the famed Rabanus Maurus. He then returned to Weissenburg, entered its Benedictine abbey, and became prefect of the abbey school and notary in 851.

At Weissenburg he started his great poem, the Book of the Gospels written in German, which took most of his life to finish. He dedicated it to King Louis the German and Bishop Salomo of Constance, and sought Bishop Liutbert of Mainz's approval in a Latin prose letter. He wrote at the wish of fellow monks and a devout lady. He hoped to displace worldly songs in favour with the people, and to bring the Gospel story home in the people's own tongue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-truchses:
Otto Truchsess von Waldburg was Cardinal-Bishop of Augsburg from 1543 to 1573, born at Castle Scheer in Swabia on 26 February 1514 and dead at Rome on 2 April 1573. He studied at Tuebingen, Padua, Pavia, and Bologna, taking his doctorate in theology at Bologna. Young canonries at Trent, Speyer, and Augsburg led to work as imperial councillor and papal chamberlain.

Elected Bishop of Augsburg on 10 May 1543, he became cardinal-priest in 1544 for settling a long dispute between emperor and pope. His diocese was in poor shape, with ignorant clergy and wide Protestant growth. He answered with visitations, edicts, synods, and better teaching, and founded the University of Dillingen and its seminary. In 1564 he handed both to the Jesuits, and from 1568 he lived wholly at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-of-midde:
Paul of Middelburg was a scientist and bishop born in 1446 at Middelburg in Zealand, then imperial land, now Dutch, and dead at Rome on 13 December 1534. After Louvain studies he held a canonry at home, then lost it, calling the loss usurpation and railing at his country as a barbarous island of sheep and craftsmen. He taught at Louvain, took a Padua science chair from Venice's Signoria in 1480, travelled Italy, and served as physician to Urbino's duke and friend to Archduke Maximilian.

Urbino gave him Saint Christopher's abbey at Castel Durante in 1488, and Maximilian backed him for Fossombrone, where he was named bishop in 1494. On appointment he destroyed early works, including a 1480 forecast censuring mathematicians, a tract on bad constellations, and an invective against a superstitious prophet. He chose an astronomical coat of arms, and in 1497 enlarged and beautified his episcopal palace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pol-de-limbou:
Pol de Limbourg was a French miniaturist, a painter of manuscript illuminations, who flourished at Paris with his two brothers around 1400. Their family name was likely Malouel, and they were nephews of Jean Malouel, court painter to the Duke of Burgundy. The name de Limbourg points to their origin near Van Eyck's country, then dependent on Burgundy.

By about 1395 they were already famous in Paris, and in 1416 they worked for the Duc de Berry on the Très Riches Heures of Chantilly. Of its two hundred odd paintings, only the first half are theirs, the rest being added fifty years later by Jean Colombe. Pol, probably the eldest and head of the workshop, likely devised the designs his brothers then executed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prince-charle: Charles d'Arenberg was definitor general and commissary of the Capuchins, and died at Brussels on 5 June 1669. He wrote Flores Seraphici, lives of eminent Capuchins from 1525 to 1612, printed at Cologne and Antwerp in two volumes in 1640. He also wrote Clypeus Seraphicus, printed at Cologne in 1643, a defence of Boverius' Annales Capucinorum. The entry cites Buchberger's handbook as its source.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratzeburg:
Ratzeburg, in Germany under Hamburg, embraced the Duchy of Lauenburg in Holstein and the Principality of Ratzeburg in Mecklenburg-Strelitz. It also took the western part of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, including Wismar but not Schwerin. This encyclopedia entry notes that the territory now lies in the Diocese of Osnabrück. Ratzeburg ranked among the dioceses formed about 1050 by Adalbert the First, Archbishop of Hamburg, who gave the new see to Saint Aristo, fresh from Jerusalem.

Aristo seems to have been little more than a wandering missionary bishop. In 1066 the Wends rebelled against their German masters. On 15 July 1066 Saint Ansuerus, Abbot of Saint George's at Ratzeburg, with several of his monks, is said to have been stoned to death. Stable organization waited until 1154, the entry notes. Histories of Lauenburg with Masch's and Neuendorff's studies of the bishopric, the latter with a map of the diocese in 1231, close the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rottenburg:
Rottenburg is a diocese in the Upper Rhine province, covering Wurtemberg and four nearby parishes. Divided into 29 districts, it contained in 1911 some 698 parishes, 19 incorporated churches, and 164 chapels. It counted 1,084 active and 75 retired clergy and 728,000 Catholics. Its cathedral chapter elects the bishops.

The bishop, dean, and six canons also form its ruling body, advised by a lay official who directs its office. State rights over sacred matters rest with a royal Catholic church council. Church schools include the priests' seminary at Rottenburg and the state-run Wilhelmsstift college at Tubingen. Boarding schools stand at Ehingen and Rottweil, and boys' schools at Rottenburg and nearby. Male orders had still not been let back into Wurtemberg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolf-of-hab:
Rudolf of Habsburg, German king, was born in 1218 and died at Speyer in 1291. Son of Albert IV and Countess Heilwige of Kiburg, he pursued independent politics after his father's death in the Holy Land. In the papal-imperial conflict he backed the Hohenstaufens, and during the interregnum he enlarged his house's power, especially in Switzerland. In his wide domains, centred on Swabia, he proved a good if stern ruler.

At Gregory X's instigation, Rudolf was chosen emperor on 1 October 1273. Six electors voted for him; Ottakar of Bohemia abstained. Towering but lean, he was a courageous warrior, skilled diplomat, stern yet genial. His realm ran from Meissen to the Adriatic, having added Austria, Styria, Carinthia, and Krain. Supported by the Church, he warred from 1276, and on the Marchfeld in 1278 Ottakar lost throne and life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-petersb:
Saint Petersburg, imperial residence and second capital of Russia, stands at the mouth of the Neva on the Gulf of Finland. In 1899, suburbs included, it counted 1,439,600 people, mostly Orthodox, with Catholics near five per cent and a large German and Polish presence. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia surveys a city built by willpower on a marsh.

Ingria, the land between Lakes Peipus and Ladoga, passed from Novgorod to Moscow, then to Sweden by the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617, until Peter the Great retook it in 1702. A year later he founded his new capital to open Russia to the Baltic and the West. The entry then traces Catholic parishes, churches, and institutions in a city where Catholics lived as a small but visible minority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salzburg:
Salzburg, an archdiocese matching the Austrian crown-land of the same name, began under Rome in the province of Noricum, south of the Danube, where Augustus built roads and towns. Christianity came with colonists, craftsmen, and soldiers, and Maximilian of Lorch counts as Noricum's first martyr. Its great entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows the land from Rome to the archbishops.

After Constantine's peace, barbarian attacks wrecked the Romanised country. Severus, who died in 482, stood as its last ray of Roman civilisation. He found a church already at Juvavum, now Salzburg, and witnessed the martyrdom of the priest-abbot Maximus. Only about 700 did Christian life return in strength, and the entry carries the story through Rupert, the prince-archbishops, and the modern archdiocese with its parishes and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saxe-altenbur:
Saxe-Altenburg, one of the Saxon duchies of eastern Thuringia on Saxony's western border, covers 511 square miles. It falls in two parts split by Reuss territory: the Ostkreis at 254 and the Westkreis at 257. In 1910 it held 216,312 people, with 5,449 Catholics, about three per cent, in 1905. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia explains a state born of a family partition.

The duchy became separate in 1826, when the extinction of the Saxe-Gotha line in 1821 split its lands among Saxon ducal lines, Altenburg falling to the Saxe-Hildburghausen line as an independent domain. Duke Ernest II, born in 1871, has ruled since 1902. The present duchy split from the old burgraviate of Altenburg, a Wettin ancestral estate, by the partition treaty of 1485, which divided Saxony's princely house into Ernestine and Albertine lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schwarzburg:
Schwarzburg names two small central German principalities, Rudolstadt and Sondershausen, joined in personal union under one ruler since 1909. Rudolstadt covers 363 square miles and held 100,712 people in 1910, split into the Upper Barony in Thuringia and the Lower Barony south of the Harz. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia counts a land where Catholics are few.

In 1905, of 96,835 Rudolstadt people, 95,641 were Lutherans, 994 Catholics, and 82 Jews, barely one per cent Catholic, up from a tenth of a per cent in 1871. The Upper Barony, centred on Rudolstadt at 280 square miles, includes the Leutenberg exclave, while the Lower Barony around Frankenhausen covers 83. Sondershausen, about 333 square miles with 89,984 people, likewise splits into two districts, and the entry maps both states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sigismond-tha:
Sigismund Thalberg, musical composer and pianist, was born at Geneva in 1812 and died at Posilipo, Italy, on 27 April 1871. The exact day of his birth is disputed. A natural son of Prince Moritz Dietrichstein, he was brought young to Vienna. At the Polytechnic Institute he befriended the young Duke of Reichstadt, whose dreams of military glory nearly drew him into a soldier's career. Mittag, a Viennese bassoonist, discovered his musical genius and saved him from that step.

He studied theory under Sechter and piano technique under Hummel, played in public at fourteen in Prince Metternich's salon, and began touring Europe in 1830. By 1834 he was court chamber musician to the emperor. For a quarter century his fame stood unrivaled save for Franz Liszt, drawing crowds in every European capital, in Brazil, and in the United States in 1857. His fantasies on operatic melodies remain his best-known works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-burchard-o:
St. Burchard of Wurzburg was first bishop of Wurzburg, born in England of Anglo-Saxon parents, date unknown. He died in Germany most probably in 754. This entry follows a boy who, after his parents' death, left home for missionary work in Germany, drawn by his countryman St. Boniface's great reputation, to whom he offered himself as an assistant. As Boniface was then an archbishop, Burchard must have begun missionary work on German soil after 732.

He soon showed himself a competent and zealous messenger of the faith. Boniface consecrated him bishop of the Wurzburg see while erecting Thuringia's mission hierarchy. The date is probably 741: on 22 October of that year, Burchard and Witta of Buraburg joined as bishops to consecrate Willibald as bishop of Eichstatt. In a letter to Boniface dated 1 April 743, Pope Zachary confirmed the founding of the new diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vergilius-:
Vergilius of Salzburg, an Irish missionary and astronomer, clashed with Boniface over baptism and the shape of the earth. In Irish Fergal, he was said to descend from Niall of the Nine Hostages and appears in the annals as abbot of Aghaboe. About 745 he left Ireland intending the Holy Land, but settled in France, welcomed by Pepin, mayor of the palace.

After two years at Cressy near Compiègne, he went to Bavaria at Duke Odilo's invitation and within a year or two became abbot of St Peter's at Salzburg. From humility he kept his orders hidden, leaving a fellow countryman, Dobdagrecus, to perform episcopal functions. His defence of a priest's garbled baptismal formula and his teaching on antipodes drew Boniface's censure. He died as bishop of Salzburg in 784.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stolberg:
Friedrich Leopold, Count zu Stolberg, was born in Holstein in 1750. He was a German poet and nobleman, famed most for his conversion to Catholicism. This entry follows him from a Copenhagen childhood among literary friends to law studies at Halle and Göttingen.

At Göttingen he joined the young poets of the Hainbund. Travels in Switzerland with Goethe came in 1775. Service under the Protestant Prince-Bishop of Lübeck followed, then marriage and writing. His slow religious journey ended in reception into the Catholic Church in 1800. That step cost him friends and stirred his sister to her own brief conversion. He died near Osnabrück in 1819.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-strasburg:
Strasburg, a German diocese answering directly to Rome, is the subject of this long historical entry. Legend puts its founding in the third or fourth century, while the first bishop known to history signed the acts of the Council of Paris in 614. Under Bishop Eddo, working with St Boniface, the diocese took the shape it largely kept through the Middle Ages.

Seven archdeaconries, gifts of mint rights and customs freedom from emperors, and the shifting fortunes of Alsace between French and German rule all fill the narrative. Reformation losses, revolutionary suppression, and the rebuilding of Catholic life in the nineteenth century bring the story near the present, with lists of bishops, churches, and schools closing the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stuhlweissenb:
Stuhlweissenburg is a Hungarian diocese, suffragan of Gran, formed in 1777 from Györ and Veszprém. Its older collegiate chapter, founded by King St Stephen in 1006, enjoyed great privileges, and its provost served as royal chancellor under thirteenth-century law. The chapter archives, once the finest in Hungary, held a copy of the Golden Bull of 1222 before Turkish invasions destroyed them.

From 1380 to 1527 the city was both coronation and burial place of Hungarian kings, and its cathedral, which kept the royal insignia, was destroyed by Turks in 1601. The diocese covers Fejér county, part of Pilis, and Csepel island in the Danube, counting 230,305 Catholics, while Budapest itself answers to Gran.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synods-of-aug:
Synods of Augsburg, convened by German bishops from Boniface's time onward, carried weight. Bishops were princes of the empire, and the emperor protected the Roman Church. Two general imperial synods met at Augsburg. The first, in August 952 under Otto the Great and Archbishop Frederick of Mainz, reformed civil and church abuses through eleven canons. Three archbishops and twenty bishops were present.

A second, called by Archbishop Anno of Cologne in October 1062, faced the empire's internal troubles and the German Church's stance toward the antipope Cadalus. Diocesan synods followed the wider German pattern. Visitation synods under bishop, archdeacon, and local lord judged and inquired. Stated synods after St Ulrich's time handled grants, privileges, and disputes. An agreement of 1389 left the city practically independent of episcopal rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thierry-of-fr:
Dominican thinker Thierry of Freiburg, philosopher and doctor of the Middle Ages, is the scholar traced here. He may or may not match Frater Theodoricus, prior of Würzburg's convent in 1283. Strasburg's Chapter General of 1293 surely made him superior general of Germany's province, a post he held till 1296. Paris heard him teach Peter Lombard's Sentences in 1297, Coblenz in 1303, Toulouse's Chapter General in 1304.

Plaisance's Chapter General of 1310 named him Vicar of the German province pending a new provincial, and his later life is unknown. A 1330 list of Dominican writers gives him thirty-one treatises, twenty-one still extant, on theology, metaphysics, and cosmology. One work above all brings him glory, a treatise on the rainbow and light that foreshadowed modern optics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-of-str:
Thomas of Strasburg, a fourteenth-century Augustinian scholar, died in 1357. Born at Hagenau or Strasburg, by differing accounts, he probably entered the Augustinian order at Strasburg and began teaching there. About 1341 he went to Paris, where he won fame as a university teacher, and in 1345 he was elected general of his order, serving until his death.

As general he revised the order's constitution, publishing the new statutes as Constitutiones Ordinis Sui, and he pushed study among his friars. In 1351 he helped found a house of studies at Verona for logic, philosophy and theology. His best known book, a commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences, appeared at Strasburg in 1490 and ran through later editions at Venice, Genoa and Geneva.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ulrich-of-bam:
Ulrich of Bamberg was a cleric of Bamberg cathedral about the year 1100, of whom little else is known. He is probably the same as the Bamberg priest of that name who died on 7 July 1127, appears often in official records, and gave large gifts to Michelsberg monastery. His work is the Codex epistolaris, a collection of letters from popes, emperors, cardinals, and princes, both churchmen and laymen.

Finished in 1125 and dedicated to Bishop Gebhard of Würzburg, the collection gathers letters from the year 900 onward. It was plainly meant to train chancellors and statesmen, giving them models for the form of letters and public documents. Many of its letters matter for history as well as for style. The entry thus preserves a rare window on how the medieval chancery learned its craft.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
For centuries Catholic cantons in Switzerland had debated a Catholic university of their own, and the need only sharpened with time. Higher schools existed solely in Protestant cantons, giving Protestants a clear intellectual lead. Yet want of funds and jealousy among the Catholic cantons kept blocking any settlement. From the start the people of Fribourg pressed hardest for a university in their town.

Out of their own resources they founded a law school in 1763, which ran until 1889 and then merged into the new university's law faculty. The entry traces the long campaign, the cantonal votes, and the eventual founding, with its faculties, professors, and bilingual character. It closes with the young university's place in Swiss Catholic life, a late answer to a long-felt want.

Heidelberg's fame rests on its university, founded in 1386 by the warlike Rupert I of Wittelsbach when he was past seventy. The city itself emerges into clear history in 1214, when Emperor Frederick II gave Duke Louis I the dignity of Count Palatine of the Rhine. From then on the Palatinate and its capital shared the fortunes of thirty counts and electors, until the settlement of 1803 at Ratisbon broke the state apart among its neighbours.

The university was modelled on Paris, the entry notes, and its early masters and students are listed with its faculties and colleges. It follows the school through humanism, the Reformation, war, and rebuilding, as Heidelberg changed hands and faiths. Readers get a full civic and academic history, with the university's scholars and its famous library woven into the town's larger story.

Würzburg's first university came from John I of Egloffstein, Bishop from 1400 to 1411, who obtained a charter from Boniface IX dated 10 December 1492. The school was modelled on Bologna and stressed theology and canon and civil law. After its founder's death it decayed, as the cathedral chapter, made up of noblemen, withdrew its support. More than a century later Bishop Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn refounded it.

On 28 March 1575 Gregory XIII issued the bull chartering the new university, with the privileges of Paris and Bologna. Its buildings rose between 1582 and 1591, and it opened on 2 January 1582. The Julius Hospital stands among its monuments. The entry follows the refounded school's faculties, its Jesuit direction, and its later history as a Bavarian university, a story of collapse and rebuilding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wuerzburg:
Wuerzburg is the Bavarian diocese suffragan to Bamberg, spanning Lower Franconia, three Upper Franconian towns, and Saxe-Meiningen enclaves. In 1911 it held ten city parishes, thirty-four rural deaneries, 447 parishes and curacies, and 712 active priests with fifty-five retired, 121 regulars, 560,000 Catholics, and about 120,000 non-Catholics. Bavaria appoints the bishop, and the chapter holds a provost, dean, eight capitulars, six prebends, and a preacher.

Training runs through the university theology faculty with eight teachers, the seminary with seventy-five students, the Chilianeum, and the house of studies. Orders in the diocese include Augustinians, Benedictines, Franciscans, Capuchins, Carmelites, Conventuals, and English Ladies. Franciscan nuns from Maria Stern and Dillingen, Carmelites, Holy Saviour sisters with 184 branch houses and 1160 sisters, and many more complete the list. Its cathedral, a Romanesque basilica from the twelfth to fourteenth centuries, holds thirty-five prince-bishop tombs, several by Riemenschneider, plus the rococo Schönborn chapel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wurtemberg:
Wurtemberg was the third largest and fourth most populous state of the German Empire, between Bavaria and Baden. Its area was 7534 square miles, and in 1910 it held 2,437,574 people, with Stuttgart as capital; in 1905 it counted 695,808 Catholics, 1,583,745 Protestants, and 12,053 Jews. Four circles divide it: Neckar at eleven percent Catholic, Black Forest at twenty-six, Jagst at thirty-two, and Danube at sixty-two. The south runs Catholic, as does most of the higher nobility.

The land grew from a countship at the Rems, Fils, and Neckar junction, named for Wirtenberc castle south of Stuttgart. Count Konrad, 1081 to 1092, heads the ruling house, and succession runs unbroken from Ulrich I, 1241 to 1265. Primogeniture came early, unlike other German states. Eberhard the Bearded became duke in 1495, and the state won electoral rank in 1803 and kingship under Napoleon in 1805. It backed Austria in 1866, then allied with Prussia and entered the Empire in 1871 with privileges like Bavaria.
doe-osti-2574056-resolving-femtosecond-p:
Final scientific and technical report DE-SC0020141, by Jeffrey Moses of Cornell University and covering August 2019 to December 2024, chases the first instants after a molecule absorbs light. Within tens to hundreds of femtoseconds, the energy is steered toward a useful change or harmlessly shed. These nonadiabatic transitions drive DNA's ultraviolet self-protection and the first step of human vision, yet no experiment had captured one completely.

The missing tool was a set of coordinated light pulses, ten femtoseconds long, spanning visible to mid-infrared wavelengths. The team developed a relatively simple way to generate them. With the source in hand, reaction paths can be followed from the moment of excitation through the conical intersection seam, where electronic states cross. A side goal is benchmarking the computer models of these molecules, so theorists learn which of their simulations to trust.
doe-osti-3005324-hydrogen-production-fro:
Michael L. Swanson of the University of North Dakota's Energy and Environmental Research Center, with Joelle Simonpietri and Jennifer Chinen, report a hydrogen project in a November 2025 final deliverable. The sponsor is the National Energy Technology Laboratory, under cooperative agreement DE-FE0032183. The idea: gasify the organic fraction of construction and demolition waste, a high-volume stream usually landfilled, and make hydrogen from the gas.

The volume is a full project record. It covers feedstock preparation with photographs, syngas cleanup equipment, greenhouse gas life-cycle analysis, and particle and fluid dynamics modeling. Appendices add a technical feasibility study and an air permit application for the partner's Hawaii site, Aloha SMRFF. The reporting period ran to November 30, 2025. Waste-to-hydrogen lives or dies on cleanup and permitting, and this record shows both sides.
doe-osti-3017351-closure-models-for-the-:
Jane Pratt, of Georgia State University and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, wrote this report, LLNL-TR-2014987, dated January 25, 2026. It develops closure models for the feedback of energetic particles on plasma turbulence. Energetic particles resonate with plasma waves, steadying some and stirring others. Their tug changes background turbulence in ways not yet fully measured or understood.

A full kinetic model would track a probability distribution for every particle in seven dimensions, which is too costly to compute directly. Pratt argues for probability density function closures, borrowed partly from reactive flow modeling. Sparse Lagrangian methods, which use far fewer tracked particles than grid points, are a core tool. Mixture models and mapping closures get detailed treatment. The stakes reach from fusion plasmas to cosmic rays and solar energetic particles. Modelers get a cheaper path to physics that brute-force simulation cannot reach.
doe-osti-3377647-slope-state-and-local-p: SLOPE got energy-planned, and this DOE slides cover state local planning. The pages detail the slope findings. The energy folks get their deck. The format was slides. The deck was energy. The SLOPE were planning. The local were state.
doe-osti-3377855-open-air-manufacturing-: Perovskites got open-air-manufactured, and this DOE text covers large-area cells. The pages detail the efficient findings. The energy folks get their data. The targets were stability cost. The data were energy. The perovskite were cells. The cost were stability.
doe-osti-3377899-use-and-siting-of-elect: Juneau EV chargers got use-sited, and this DOE text covers Alaska stations. The pages detail the charging findings. The transport folks get their data. The siting was use. The data were transport. The Juneau were stations. The charging were findings.
history-and-comprehensive-description-of:
James William Head wrote this history of Loudoun County, Virginia, copyrighted in 1908. Head calls the book the single ambition of his life. He gives it to his mother, whose love for Loudoun matched his own. A quoted tribute praises the county as country life at its purest.

Head traces the county from its making in 1757, when Fairfax was divided. Bounds along the Potomac, Bull Run, and Ashby's Gap are set out in detail. Land, towns, farms, and folk fill the long description. Local readers get a proud, full record of one Virginia county's growth and character.
nasa-tm-19650010113-an-experimental-exam:
A sounding rocket flight from Fort Churchill on September 4, 1963, carried this cosmic ray experiment above the atmosphere. Large sheets of nuclear emulsion were extended from the sides of the rocket during its time outside the air. Passing cosmic ray nuclei left tracks in those sheets. The author sought heavy nuclei at low energies, below the reach of balloon-borne experiments of the day.

A finite flux of heavy nuclei was in fact detected, the author reports. Separate fluxes are given for the heavier and lighter nuclei groups in the energy ranges studied. Light nuclei in a lower charge range were also seen. Direct counts of this kind tested ideas about where cosmic rays come from and how they travel.
podcast-joerogan-UAx1Sq6usRg:
Raghunath Cappo joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1430. Cappo fronted hardcore punk bands before becoming a yoga teacher and spiritual guide, a path that earned him the label punk-rock monk. His life crosses two worlds Rogan respects: the stage and the mat.

He tells Rogan about the years of touring, addiction, and collapse that led him to Indian temples and daily practice. The talk covers chanting, discipline, and what a seeker owes his teachers. The episode is a conversion story told without soft edges, by a man whose tattoos and prayer beads tell it before he speaks.
podcast-joerogan-xJ6Ym719urg:
Mycologist Paul Stamets talks mushrooms with Joe Rogan in episode 1385 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Stamets has spent his life studying fungi and arguing they can heal people and the planet. This early, spore-filled session became a classic among his fans.

Stamets explains mycelium, the vast fungal web under forests that he calls nature's internet. He covers psilocybin research, bees saved by fungi, and his famous stack of supplements. Rogan shares his own respect for mushrooms and asks bold questions. The myco-curious get a rich tour from the field's most famous voice.
the-gist-of-swedenborg:
Julian K. Smyth and William F. Wunsch compiled The Gist of Swedenborg. The Swedenborg Foundation printed it in New York in 1920. A life note opens the book. Emanuel Swedenborg was born at Stockholm on January 29, 1688. His father was a Lutheran clergyman. He later became Bishop of Skara.

The note traces his study at Upsala. It traces five years in England, France, Holland, and Germany. He worked in mathematics and astronomy. He met Flamsteed and Halley. He wrote on mining, geology, chemistry, and invention. He also sat in the Swedish Diet. His Principia capped his science work. The gist that follows draws the core of his later religious thought. It gives that thought in short form for new readers.
the-man-that-corrupted-hadleyburg:
Mark Twain's The Man That Corrupted Hadleyburg opens on a town proud of one possession above all others: its honesty. Hadleyburg kept its reputation unsmirched for three generations, taught honest dealing to babies in the cradle, and kept temptation away from its young so their honesty could harden into bone. Neighboring towns sneered and called it vanity, yet admitted that a young man from Hadleyburg needed no other recommendation.

Then Hadleyburg offended a passing stranger, without knowing or caring. The bitter man nursed the injury for a year, rejecting plan after plan because each hurt too few people. What he wanted was a scheme that would comprehend the entire town and let no one escape. At last the idea lit his head with evil joy: he would corrupt the town. Six months later he arrived at the bank cashier's house at night, carrying a heavy sack.
tom-swift-in-the-city-of-gold-or-marvelo: Marvelous Adventures Underground await in the Tom Swift city of gold story by Victor Appleton, presented through twenty-five chapter headings. Wonderful news, an unsuspected listener, and Andy whitewashed open the book. News from Africa and a warning about head-hunters follow a perilous flight. Later headings promise a golden image, a map on gold, a ruined temple, an underground river, and the city itself with its big image. Chapter one is announced without text following. The contents list alone is present here.
